question: On 16 March 1964, Türkiye violated the 1923 Treaty of Lausanne by expelling the Greek population from Istanbul. Under the treaty, all members of the Greek ethnic minority who were permanent residents on 30 October 1918 had the right to remain as établis.

However, Türkiye, a founding member of the UN and a signatory of the European Convention on Human Rights (Rome, 1950), failed to honour its promise to protect the rights of the Greek minority in Istanbul. The expelled were treated as enemies of the state and their properties confiscated until 1987 when Türkiye’s candidacy for EU membership forced Turgut Özal’s government to lift this measure.

The Greek minority has dwindled from 125 000 people in 1923 to fewer than 1 000 people today, most of whom are aged over 60, live outside the city (99 %) and endure repressive measures and the confiscation of property belonging to charitable foundations and private individuals.

With the expulsions of 1964-1965 the minority population dropped to 30 000 people and in 10 years it will drop even further to just a few hundred. In view of this, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
In the context of Türkiye’s accession path, will the issue of the Greek ethnic minority be put on the table?
Will it raise the issue of the violations made against the charitable foundations of the Greek ethnic minority in Istanbul?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (24.7.2024) Respect for human dignity, freedom, democracy, equality, the rule of law and respect for human rights, including the rights of persons belonging to minorities, are founding EU values that also lie at the heart of the enlargement process. In its political engagement with Türkiye, the Commission has consistently attached great importance to these matters.

In its annual reports on Türkiye, the Commission regularly assesses the situation of minorities including issues linked to religious freedom, religious monuments, property rights, hate crime and freedom of association.

In the 2023 report1, the Commission highlighted the various difficulties that persons belonging to ethnic and national minorities face in Turkey, noting that hate speech and hate crimes, notably against Christians, Protestants, Jews and Alevis, continued to be a serious issue.

The Commission called Türkiye to improve the legislative framework and its implementation to effectively tackle all forms of racism and discrimination to ensure the protection of minorities, including concerning legislation on property rights for non-Muslim minorities. Decisions in cases related to the property of religious communities still need to be implemented.

The EU is committed to developing a culture of inclusive tolerance both in the EU, and in the candidate countries for EU accession. In this context, the EU encourages and supports interreligious dialogue aimed at increasing mutual understanding and respect. The Commission will continue closely monitoring the situation and addressing issues of concern in its bilateral contacts with the Turkish authorities.
